en-B2-0.b:
The third conditional imagines a different past (it didn't happen): If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

  • If I had studied, I would have passed. (I didn't study, I failed.)
  • If you had told me, I could have helped.

Mixed conditionals combine times:

  • Past condition → present result: If + past perfect, would + verb: If I had taken that job, I would be rich now.
  • Present condition → past result: If + past simple, would have + participle: If I spoke Dutch, I would have understood the meeting yesterday.

Formal inversion (no if): Had I known, I would have come.

Common mistake: « If I would have known » → If I had known; « I would have came » → I would have come.
en-B2-0.t:
Le troisième conditionnel imagine un passé différent (qui n'a pas eu lieu) : If + past perfect, would have + participe passé (= si + plus-que-parfait, conditionnel passé).

  • If I had studied, I would have passed. (Je n'ai pas étudié, j'ai échoué.)
  • If you had told me, I could have helped.

Les conditionnels mixtes combinent les temps :

  • Condition passée → résultat présent : If + past perfect, would + verbe : If I had taken that job, I would be rich now.
  • Condition présente → résultat passé : If + prétérit, would have + participe : If I spoke Dutch, I would have understood the meeting yesterday.

Inversion soutenue (sans if) : Had I known, I would have come. (Si j'avais su…)

Erreur fréquente : « If I would have known » → If I had known ; « I would have came » → I would have come.
e: If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the train.
If she had studied, she would have passed.
If I had learnt Dutch as a child, I would be fluent now.
Had I known, I would have called you.
If he weren't so shy, he would have spoken to her.
q: If I ___ known, I would have come.
If you had told me, I ___ helped.
If I had taken that job, I ___ rich now. (mixed)
If she ___ Dutch, she would have understood. (present ability)
If we had left earlier, we ___ the train.
If I would have time, I'd have helped.
If I had had time, I would have helped.
If I had time, I would have help.

en-B2-1.b:
wish / if only express regret or a desire for things to be different.

about…structureexample
the presentwish + past simpleI wish I spoke Dutch. (I don't)
the pastwish + past perfectI wish I had studied harder. (I didn't)
annoying behaviour / future changewish + wouldI wish you would stop talking.
  • If only is stronger: If only I had more time!
  • With be: I wish I were taller (formal; was in speech).
  • could for ability: I wish I could swim.
  • Not with yourself + would: « I wish I would… » → I wish I could…

Common mistake: « I wish I have more money » → I wish I had more money.
en-B2-1.t:
wish / if only expriment un regret ou le désir que les choses soient différentes.

à propos de…structureexemple
le présentwish + prétéritI wish I spoke Dutch. (J'aimerais parler néerlandais — je ne le parle pas)
le passéwish + past perfectI wish I had studied harder. (Je regrette de ne pas avoir…)
comportement agaçant / changement futurwish + wouldI wish you would stop talking.
  • If only est plus fort (si seulement) : If only I had more time!
  • Avec be : I wish I were taller (soutenu ; was à l'oral).
  • could pour une capacité : I wish I could swim.
  • Pas avec soi-même + would : « I wish I would… » → I wish I could…

Erreur fréquente : « I wish I have more money » → I wish I had more money.
e: I wish I lived closer to the sea.
I wish I had listened to my parents.
If only it would stop raining!
She wishes she could speak Dutch fluently.
I wish you wouldn't leave your clothes on the floor.
q: I wish I ___ harder at school. (past)
She wishes she ___ that. (past regret, say)
I wish I would be rich.
If only I ___ about it earlier! (know, past)

en-B2-2.b:
Advanced passive structures are common in news, reports and formal English.

  • It is said / believed / thought / reported that…: It is believed that the minister will resign.
  • Subject + is said / believed + to-infinitive: The minister is believed to be resigning. Past: He is thought to have left the country.
  • Passive with two objects: I was given a prize. (A prize was given to me.)
  • Passive infinitive / gerund: I hope to be chosen. She hates being told what to do.
  • get passive (informal, often negative events): He got fired. My bike got stolen.
  • Passive with modals (past): It should have been done yesterday.

Common mistake: « He is said that he is rich » → He is said to be rich / It is said that he is rich.
en-B2-2.t:
Les structures passives avancées sont courantes dans la presse, les rapports et l'anglais formel.

  • It is said / believed / thought / reported that… (On dit / On pense que…) : It is believed that the minister will resign.
  • Sujet + is said / believed + to-infinitif : The minister is believed to be resigning. Passé : He is thought to have left the country. (On pense qu'il a quitté…)
  • Passif avec deux compléments : I was given a prize. (On m'a donné un prix)
  • Infinitif / gérondif passif : I hope to be chosen. She hates being told what to do.
  • Passif avec get (familier, souvent événements négatifs) : He got fired. My bike got stolen.
  • Passif avec modal (passé) : It should have been done yesterday. (Ça aurait dû être fait)

Erreur fréquente : « He is said that he is rich » → He is said to be rich / It is said that he is rich.
e: It is said that the castle is haunted.
The suspect is believed to have fled abroad.
I was offered a new job last week.
She hates being interrupted.
The report should have been sent yesterday.
q: I ___ a new laptop by my company.
I hope ___ for the team. (choose, passive)

en-B2-3.b:
The causative says that someone else does something for you (often a service).

  • have + object + past participle: I had my hair cut. (= the hairdresser cut it, not me) · We're having the house painted.
  • get + object + past participle (more informal): I need to get my car repaired.
  • Also for bad experiences: She had her bag stolen.

To say who does it:

  • have + person + base verb: I'll have the technician check it.
  • get + person + to + verb (persuade): I got my brother to help me.
  • make + person + base verb (force): The teacher made us rewrite it.
  • let + person + base verb (allow): My boss let me leave early.

Common mistake: « I cut my hair » (when the hairdresser did it) → I had my hair cut.
en-B2-3.t:
Le causatif dit que quelqu'un d'autre fait quelque chose pour toi (souvent un service) = faire faire.

  • have + objet + participe passé : I had my hair cut. (Je me suis fait couper les cheveux — par le coiffeur) · We're having the house painted.
  • get + objet + participe passé (plus familier) : I need to get my car repaired.
  • Aussi pour les mauvaises expériences : She had her bag stolen. (Elle s'est fait voler son sac)

Pour dire qui le fait :

  • have + personne + verbe de base : I'll have the technician check it.
  • get + personne + to + verbe (persuader) : I got my brother to help me.
  • make + personne + verbe de base (obliger) : The teacher made us rewrite it.
  • let + personne + verbe de base (laisser, permettre) : My boss let me leave early.

Erreur fréquente : « I cut my hair » (quand c'est le coiffeur) → I had my hair cut.
e: I had my hair cut yesterday.
We're getting the kitchen renovated.
She had her phone stolen on the train.
I got my friend to proofread my CV.
My parents never let me stay out late.
q: I ___ my car ___ last week. (repair, by a mechanic)
The teacher made us ___ it again. (write)
"Je me suis fait couper les cheveux" = ___

en-B2-4.b:
The future perfect = will have + past participle. It says that an action will be finished before a certain moment in the future.

  • By 2030, I will have learnt three languages.
  • Call me at 6; I'll have finished work by then.
  • By the time you arrive, we will have eaten.

Key words: by (+ time), by then, by the time, before, in two years' time.

Future perfect continuous = will have been + -ing (duration up to a future point): In June, I will have been living in Belgium for five years.

Negative: I won't have finished by Friday.

Common mistake: « By the time you will arrive » → By the time you arrive (present after time words).
en-B2-4.t:
Le futur antérieur = will have + participe passé. Il dit qu'une action sera terminée avant un moment futur.

  • By 2030, I will have learnt three languages. (D'ici 2030, j'aurai appris…)
  • Call me at 6; I'll have finished work by then.
  • By the time you arrive, we will have eaten.

Mots-clés : by (+ moment, d'ici), by then, by the time (au moment où), before, in two years' time.

Futur antérieur continu = will have been + -ing (durée jusqu'à un point futur) : In June, I will have been living in Belgium for five years. (En juin, cela fera cinq ans que je vis…)

Négation : I won't have finished by Friday.

Erreur fréquente : « By the time you will arrive » → By the time you arrive (présent après les mots de temps, contrairement au français).
e: By next year, I will have finished my studies.
Don't worry, I'll have fixed it by tonight.
By the time we get there, the film will have started.
In May, we'll have been married for ten years.
She won't have arrived before midnight.
q: By the time you ___, we'll have eaten.
In June, I ___ in Belgium for 5 years. (live, duration)
Call at 6; I'll have ___ work by then.
Key word for the future perfect: ___
By the end of the day, she ___ 100 emails. (write)

en-B2-5.b:
Participle clauses make sentences shorter and more elegant, especially in writing. The subject must be the same as in the main clause.

  • Present participle (-ing) = active, same time or reason: Feeling tired, I went to bed. (= Because I felt tired) · Walking home, I met Tom. (= While I was walking)
  • Past participle = passive: Built in 1900, the house needs repairs. (= It was built…) · Asked about the plan, he refused to comment.
  • Perfect participle (having + participle) = action before: Having finished the report, she went home.
  • Instead of relative clauses: The man sitting there is my uncle. Products made in Belgium…

Common mistake (dangling participle): « Walking in the park, the rain started » (the rain wasn't walking!) → Walking in the park, I got caught in the rain.
en-B2-5.t:
Les propositions participiales rendent les phrases plus courtes et élégantes, surtout à l'écrit. Le sujet doit être le même que celui de la principale.

  • Participe présent (-ing) = actif, simultanéité ou cause : Feeling tired, I went to bed. (= Comme j'étais fatigué) · Walking home, I met Tom. (= En rentrant à pied)
  • Participe passé = passif : Built in 1900, the house needs repairs. (= Construite en 1900…) · Asked about the plan, he refused to comment.
  • Participe parfait (having + participe) = action antérieure : Having finished the report, she went home. (Ayant terminé…)
  • À la place d'une relative : The man sitting there is my uncle. Products made in Belgium…

Erreur fréquente (participe « suspendu ») : « Walking in the park, the rain started » (la pluie ne se promenait pas !) → Walking in the park, I got caught in the rain.
e: Feeling hungry, we stopped at a café.
Having lived in Ghent, she speaks Dutch well.
Written in 1850, the novel is still popular.
The woman standing by the door is my manager.
Not knowing what to say, he kept quiet.
q: ___ the report, she went home. (finish, before)
The man ___ there is my uncle. (sit)
___ what to say, he left. (not know)
___ by the news, she started crying. (shock)

en-B2-6.b:
Modal + have + past participle talks about the past: regrets, criticism, deductions.

  • should have / shouldn't have: regret, criticism: I should have studied more. You shouldn't have said that.
  • could have: a possibility that didn't happen: You could have called me! (but you didn't)
  • would have: imagined result: I would have helped you.
  • might / may have: possible past: She might have missed the bus.
  • must have: almost sure: He must have forgotten.
  • can't / couldn't have: impossible: He can't have seen us.
  • needn't have: unnecessary but done: You needn't have brought a gift.

In speech: should've, could've, would've [ʃʊdəv]. Never write « should of ».

Common mistake: « I should have went » → I should have gone; « You must have to… » → You must have + participle.
en-B2-6.t:
Modal + have + participe passé parle du passé : regrets, reproches, déductions.

  • should have / shouldn't have : regret, reproche (j'aurais dû) : I should have studied more. You shouldn't have said that.
  • could have : une possibilité non réalisée (tu aurais pu) : You could have called me!
  • would have : résultat imaginé : I would have helped you.
  • might / may have : passé possible : She might have missed the bus. (Elle a peut-être raté…)
  • must have : presque sûr (a dû) : He must have forgotten.
  • can't / couldn't have : impossible : He can't have seen us.
  • needn't have : pas nécessaire mais fait : You needn't have brought a gift. (Il ne fallait pas…)

À l'oral : should've, could've, would've [ʃʊdəv]. N'écris jamais « should of ».

Erreur fréquente : « I should have went » → I should have gone.
e: I should have listened to you.
You could have told me earlier!
She must have left already.
He can't have finished so quickly.
You needn't have waited for me.
q: Unnecessary: You ___ brought food; we had plenty.

en-B2-7.b:
Linkers of contrast and concession help you present opposing ideas — essential for debates and essays.

  • although / even though + clause: Although it was late, we continued. (even though is stronger)
  • despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite the rain, we went out. In spite of being tired, she worked. (Never « despite of »)
  • however (new sentence, with commas): It's expensive. However, it's worth it.
  • whereas / while: direct comparison: I like tea, whereas my wife prefers coffee.
  • nevertheless / nonetheless (formal): The plan is risky; nevertheless, we'll try.
  • but / yet: simple yet effective.
  • even if (hypothetical): I'll go even if it rains.

Common mistake: « Despite it was raining » → Although it was raining / Despite the rain; « despite of » → despite / in spite of.
en-B2-7.t:
Les connecteurs d'opposition et de concession permettent de présenter des idées contraires — essentiels pour débattre et rédiger.

  • although / even though (bien que) + proposition : Although it was late, we continued. (even though est plus fort)
  • despite / in spite of (malgré) + nom ou -ing : Despite the rain, we went out. In spite of being tired, she worked. (Jamais « despite of »)
  • however (cependant ; nouvelle phrase, avec virgules) : It's expensive. However, it's worth it.
  • whereas / while (alors que) : comparaison directe : I like tea, whereas my wife prefers coffee.
  • nevertheless / nonetheless (néanmoins, soutenu) : The plan is risky; nevertheless, we'll try.
  • but / yet : simple yet effective (simple mais efficace).
  • even if (même si, hypothétique) : I'll go even if it rains.

Erreur fréquente : « Despite it was raining » → Although it was raining / Despite the rain ; « despite of » → despite / in spite of.
e: Although I was tired, I finished the report.
Despite the traffic, we arrived on time.
The flat is small. However, it's very central.
I prefer the city, whereas my partner loves the countryside.
I'll go out even if it rains.
q: ___ it was raining, we went out.
I like tea, ___ he likes coffee.
